Conversely, multiplying or dividing two integers with opposite signs (one positive and one negative) yields a negative integer, which is a fundamental rule applied in all advanced algebraic calculations. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step.

lessons.title: Properties of Operations on Integers
lessons.explanation: Operations on integers exhibit essential mathematical properties that simplify complex arithmetic. These include closure (results are always integers), commutativity (order of addition or multiplication does not change the result), associativity (grouping does not affect the outcome), and the distributive property of multiplication over addition. Understanding these properties allows students to solve algebraic expressions quickly, logically, and with minimal errors. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step.

Class 7 - Mathematics - Fractions and De.content: This chapter takes you deeper into the study of Fractions and Decimals, which are critical for measuring parts of a whole in science, engineering, and daily life. You will learn how to add, subtract, multiply, and divide fractional parts and decimal numbers, helping you make precise calculations in real-world scenarios.

lessons.title: Types of Fractions and Conversion
lessons.explanation: Fractions represent parts of a whole and are classified into three types. Proper fractions have a smaller numerator than denominator. Improper fractions have a larger numerator, representing values greater than one, which can be converted into mixed fractions containing a whole number and a proper fraction. Finding equivalent fractions allows us to easily compare, order, and calculate fractional values. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step.

lessons.title: Multiplication and Division of Fractions
lessons.explanation: Multiplying fractions involves multiplying their numerators and denominators straight across to find the product. To divide fractions, we multiply the first fraction by the reciprocal (the inverted form) of the second fraction. This division rule is highly useful in calculating rates, scaling recipes, and dividing resources into equal parts, turning abstract fraction mathematics into a practical real-world skill. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step.

lessons.title: Understanding Decimals and Place Value
lessons.explanation: Decimals represent fractions with denominators that are powers of ten, using a decimal point to separate whole numbers from fractional parts. In the decimal place value system, values to the right of the point represent tenths, hundredths, and thousandths. This standard system is used globally for recording financial transactions, measuring physical dimensions in metric units, and expressing high-precision scientific data. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step.

lessons.title: Operations on Decimals: Multiplication and Division
lessons.explanation: Multiplying decimals requires calculating the product as whole numbers and then placing the decimal point based on the total decimal places in the original numbers. To divide decimals by another decimal, we multiply both by a power of ten to make the divisor a whole number first. Mastering these arithmetic rules is essential for managing daily activities like budgeting, chemistry measurements, and physics calculations. Compare two different examples so you can see what changes and what always stays the same.

Class 7 - Mathematics - Data Handling.content: Welcome to the study of Data Handling, where we learn how to collect, organize, and analyze information to draw meaningful conclusions. This chapter introduces essential statistical tools like arithmetic mean, median, mode, and range to summarize data. You will also learn to read bar graphs and calculate probabilities, helping you make informed decisions.

lessons.title: Collecting and Organizing Data
lessons.explanation: Before analyzing information, we must collect relevant raw data systematically. Geographers and scientists gather measurements and organize them in structured tables using tally marks to find frequency. This initial step of data organization makes chaotic raw numbers easy to read, compare, and analyze, laying a solid foundation for calculating averages and constructing visual graphs. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step. This habit builds accuracy and confidence for harder exercises.

lessons.title: Mean, Median, and Mode
lessons.explanation: Central tendency represents the central value of a data set. The arithmetic mean is calculated by dividing the sum of all observations by their total number. The mode is the value that appears most frequently in the data, while the median is the exact middle value when observations are arranged in ascending order, providing different ways to summarize data. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step.

lessons.title: Understanding Range and Bar Graphs
lessons.explanation: The range of a data set is the mathematical difference between the highest and lowest values, showing the spread of the data. Bar graphs represent organized data visually using rectangular bars of uniform width. In Class Seven, we also study double bar graphs, which allow us to compare two different data sets simultaneously, like seasonal rainfall differences. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step.

lessons.title: Chance and Probability
lessons.explanation: Probability is the mathematical measure of how likely an event is to occur in daily life. Events are classified as certain to happen, impossible, or having a fifty-fifty chance. We calculate basic probability as a fraction by dividing the number of favorable outcomes by the total number of possible outcomes, helping us make predictions under uncertainty. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step.

Class 7 - Mathematics - Simple Equations.content: This chapter introduces the powerful mathematical tool of Simple Equations, which allows us to solve mysteries and real-world puzzles using algebraic symbols. You will learn how to construct equations from word problems and solve them by performing operations on both sides. Mastering equations develops logical thinking and simplifies advanced scientific calculations.

lessons.title: Setting Up an Equation
lessons.explanation: An algebraic equation is a mathematical statement showing that two expressions are equal. It uses constants, which have fixed values, and variables, represented by letters like x or y, which can take different values. Setting up an equation involves translating a word problem into a symbolic mathematical phrase where an unknown quantity is equated to a known value. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step.

lessons.title: Solving Equations by Balancing
lessons.explanation: An equation acts exactly like a traditional weighing balance. To maintain perfect equality, whatever mathematical operation we perform on the left-hand side must also be performed on the right-hand side. By adding, subtracting, multiplying, or dividing the exact same number on both sides of the equal sign, we can slowly isolate the variable and find its value. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step.

lessons.title: The Method of Transposition
lessons.explanation: Transposition is a faster, highly efficient method for solving simple equations. It involves moving a term from one side of the equation to the other by changing its sign to the opposite operation. A positive term becomes negative upon transposition, a negative term becomes positive, multiplication turns into division, and division turns into multiplication, simplifying calculations. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step.

lessons.title: Applications to Real-Life Problems
lessons.explanation: Simple equations are highly useful for solving practical real-world problems. We can translate statements about ages, shopping prices, geometry dimensions, or number puzzles into algebraic equations. By solving these equations using balancing or transposition, we can find the exact value of unknown quantities in daily life, demonstrating the practical power of mathematics. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step. This habit builds accuracy and confidence for harder exercises.

Class 7 - Mathematics - Lines and Angles.content: Explore the geometry of Lines and Angles, which forms the building blocks of architecture, art, and natural patterns. In this chapter, you will learn about complementary, supplementary, adjacent, and vertically opposite angles. You will also study how parallel lines interact with intersecting transversal lines, discovering the universal rules of spatial relationships.

lessons.title: Pairs of Angles
lessons.explanation: Geometric angles often exist in related pairs. Complementary angles are two angles whose sum equals exactly ninety degrees, while supplementary angles are two angles whose sum equals one hundred and eighty degrees. Adjacent angles share a common vertex and arm but have no common interior points, helping us study how lines meet and divide space. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step.

lessons.title: Intersecting and Vertically Opposite Angles
lessons.explanation: When two straight lines cross each other, they are called intersecting lines, and the point where they cross is the vertex. This intersection forms four angles, where the angles opposite to each other are called vertically opposite angles. Mathematically, vertically opposite angles are always perfectly equal to each other, a rule used in geometric proofs. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step.

lessons.title: Transversal of Parallel Lines
lessons.explanation: A transversal is a straight line that intersects two or more lines at distinct points. When a transversal intersects two parallel lines, it creates special angle pairs. The corresponding angles are equal, the alternate interior angles are equal, and the interior angles on the same side of the transversal add up to one hundred and eighty degrees. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step.

lessons.title: Geometric Proofs and Applications
lessons.explanation: The mathematical relationships between lines and angles are applied extensively in our daily lives. Engineers, architects, and designers use these angle rules to build stable bridges, design straight roads, construct houses, and create beautiful patterns. Mastering these theorems allows us to calculate unknown angles in complex structural designs using logic. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step. This habit builds accuracy and confidence for harder exercises.

Class 7 - Mathematics - The Triangle and.content: Triangles are the strongest, most stable shapes in engineering and nature. This chapter teaches you the key properties of triangles, focusing on their medians, altitudes, and angle sum relationships. You will also discover the exterior angle property, inequality rules of side lengths, and the famous Pythagorean theorem for right-angled triangles.

lessons.title: Medians and Altitudes of Triangles
lessons.explanation: A median is a line segment connecting a triangle's vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side, dividing the triangle into equal areas. An altitude is a perpendicular segment drawn from a vertex to the opposite side, representing the height of the triangle. Every triangle has exactly three medians and three altitudes intersecting at central points. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step.

lessons.title: Angle Sum and Exterior Angle Properties
lessons.explanation: Triangles possess two crucial angle properties. The angle sum property states that the sum of all three interior angles of a triangle is always exactly one hundred and eighty degrees. The exterior angle property states that any exterior angle of a triangle is equal to the sum of its two interior opposite angles, allowing us to find unknown angles. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step.

lessons.title: Triangle Inequality Property
lessons.explanation: The side lengths of a triangle must follow a strict mathematical rule to form a closed shape. The triangle inequality property states that the sum of the lengths of any two sides of a triangle must always be strictly greater than the length of the remaining third side, a rule crucial for structural stability. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step. This habit builds accuracy and confidence for harder exercises.

lessons.title: Pythagoras Property in Right Triangles
lessons.explanation: In a right-angled triangle, the side opposite to the ninety-degree angle is the hypotenuse. The Pythagoras property states that the square of the length of the hypotenuse is equal to the sum of the squares of the lengths of the other two sides, a fundamental rule used globally in navigation, construction, and geometry. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step. This habit builds accuracy and confidence for harder exercises.

Class 7 - Mathematics - Congruence of Tr.content: Congruence is the mathematical concept of exact duplication, where two geometric figures have identical shapes and sizes. This chapter focuses on the rules that determine when two triangles are congruent. By understanding these criteria, you will learn to verify designs, ensure manufacturing precision, and solve complex geometric proofs.

lessons.title: Understanding Congruence of Figures
lessons.explanation: Two geometric figures are congruent if they have the exact same shape and size. If you place one figure on top of the other and they cover each other perfectly, they are congruent. This concept is used in manufacturing identical parts, printing stamps, and designing repeating architectural structures. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step. Practice it once with a neat diagram or number line.

lessons.title: SSS and SAS Congruence Criteria
lessons.explanation: The SSS (Side-Side-Side) rule states that two triangles are congruent if all three sides of one triangle are equal to the corresponding three sides of the other. The SAS (Side-Angle-Side) rule states that two triangles are congruent if two sides and the included angle of one match the other. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step. Practice it once with a neat diagram or number line.

lessons.title: ASA and AAS Congruence Criteria
lessons.explanation: The ASA (Angle-Side-Angle) criterion establishes that two triangles are congruent if two angles and the included side of one are equal to the corresponding parts of the other. The AAS (Angle-Angle-Side) rule is a variation proving congruence when any two angles and a non-included side match. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step. Compare two different examples so you can see what changes and what always stays the same.

lessons.title: RHS Congruence Rule for Right Triangles
lessons.explanation: The RHS (Right angle-Hypotenuse-Side) congruence criterion applies specifically to right-angled triangles. It states that two right-angled triangles are congruent if the hypotenuse and one side of one triangle are equal to the hypotenuse and corresponding side of the other, ensuring perfect structural symmetry. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step. Compare two different examples so you can see what changes and what always stays the same.

Class 7 - Mathematics - Comparing Quanti.content: In our daily lives, we constantly compare sizes, weights, and prices. This chapter teaches you the practical mathematical tools of ratios, proportions, percentages, and simple interest. You will learn to solve real-world financial problems involving buying, selling, discounts, and compound comparisons, making you smart with numbers and money.

lessons.title: Ratios, Rates, and Unitary Method
lessons.explanation: A ratio compares two quantities of the same units by division, showing how many times one is larger than the other. When two ratios are equal, they form a proportion. The unitary method allows us to find the value of a single unit first and then multiply to solve rate problems. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step. This habit builds accuracy and confidence for harder exercises.

lessons.title: Percentages and Their Conversions
lessons.explanation: Percentage means parts per hundred, represented by the symbol %. We convert fractions, decimals, and ratios into percentages by multiplying them by one hundred, and convert percentages back into decimals or fractions by dividing by one hundred, which is crucial for analyzing test scores and sales taxes. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step. Practice it once with a neat diagram or number line.

lessons.title: Profit, Loss, and Discount
lessons.explanation: Commercial math involves calculating profit and loss. Profit occurs when the selling price is higher than the cost price, while loss occurs when it is lower. We calculate these as percentages of the cost price. Discounts are deductions made from the marked price to attract customers. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step. Compare two different examples so you can see what changes and what always stays the same.

lessons.title: Understanding Simple Interest
lessons.explanation: Simple interest is the extra money paid for borrowing or lending principal money over time. It is calculated using the formula: Principal multiplied by Rate of interest multiplied by Time, divided by one hundred. Understanding interest helps us manage bank savings accounts, personal loans, and financial investments. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step. Practice it once with a neat diagram or number line.

Class 7 - Mathematics - Rational Numbers.content: Rational numbers extend our number system to include fractional values that can be expressed as a ratio of two integers. This chapter defines rational numbers, shows their representation on a number line, and explains how to compare them. You will also learn to perform basic arithmetic operations on rational numbers.

lessons.title: Introduction to Rational Numbers
lessons.explanation: A rational number is any number that can be written in the form p/q, where p and q are integers and q is not equal to zero. It includes positive fractions, negative fractions, whole numbers, and zero. Rational numbers are essential for expressing values that lie between whole integers. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step. Practice it once with a neat diagram or number line.

lessons.title: Equivalent Rationals and Standard Form
lessons.explanation: We find equivalent rational numbers by multiplying or dividing the numerator and denominator by the same non-zero integer. A rational number is in its standard form when its denominator is positive and the numerator and denominator share no common factors other than one, simplifying mathematical operations. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step. Compare two different examples so you can see what changes and what always stays the same.

lessons.title: Comparing Rational Numbers
lessons.explanation: To compare two rational numbers, we first convert them to equivalent forms with a common positive denominator. This allows us to place them accurately on a number line. Between any two rational numbers, there are infinitely many other rational numbers, showing the continuous nature of our system. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step. Practice it once with a neat diagram or number line.

lessons.title: Operations on Rational Numbers
lessons.explanation: Adding, subtracting, multiplying, and dividing rational numbers follow fraction rules. For addition and subtraction, we use the Least Common Multiple (LCM) of denominators. For multiplication, we multiply numerators and denominators across, while division involves multiplying the first rational number by the reciprocal of the second divisor. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step. Compare two different examples so you can see what changes and what always stays the same.

Class 7 - Mathematics - Practical Geomet.content: Practical Geometry is the hands-on art of constructing accurate geometric figures using a ruler and a compass. In this chapter, you will learn the precise steps to draw parallel lines and construct different types of triangles based on side lengths and angle measurements, developing visual-spatial intelligence and precision.

lessons.title: Constructing Parallel Lines
lessons.explanation: Using a ruler and a compass, we can construct a line parallel to a given line through an external point. This construction is based on the alternate interior angle property. By drawing a transversal and copying the angle at the external point, we create parallel lines accurately. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step. Practice it once with a neat diagram or number line.

lessons.title: Constructing Triangles: SSS Criterion
lessons.explanation: To construct a triangle using the Side-Side-Side (SSS) rule, we are given three side lengths. We draw the base segment using a ruler, then use a compass adjusted to the other side lengths to draw intersecting arcs, locating the third vertex with absolute precision. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step. Compare two different examples so you can see what changes and what always stays the same.

lessons.title: Constructing Triangles: SAS and ASA Criteria
lessons.explanation: For the SAS (Side-Angle-Side) construction, we draw a side, construct the specified angle using a protractor or compass, and mark the second side. For the ASA (Angle-Side-Angle) construction, we draw the base side and construct two angles at its endpoints, intersecting their arms. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step. Compare two different examples so you can see what changes and what always stays the same.

lessons.title: Constructing Right-Angled Triangles: RHS
lessons.explanation: Using the RHS (Right angle-Hypotenuse-Side) criterion, we construct right-angled triangles. We draw the given leg, construct a ninety-degree perpendicular angle at one endpoint, and use a compass set to the hypotenuse length to draw an arc intersecting the perpendicular line, completing the right triangle. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step. Compare two different examples so you can see what changes and what always stays the same.

Class 7 - Mathematics - Perimeter and Ar.content: This chapter teaches you how to measure the boundaries and surface space of two-dimensional shapes. You will explore formulas for calculating the perimeter and area of squares, rectangles, triangles, parallelograms, and circles. These measurement skills are essential for carpentry, farming, construction, and art projects.

lessons.title: Area of Triangles and Parallelograms
lessons.explanation: The area of a parallelogram is calculated by multiplying its base by its perpendicular height. Since a diagonal divides a parallelogram into two congruent triangles, the mathematical formula for the area of a triangle is exactly half of base multiplied by height, which is used in architectural designs. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step. Practice it once with a neat diagram or number line.

lessons.title: Circumference of a Circle
lessons.explanation: The boundary of a circular region is called its circumference. The ratio of the circumference to its diameter is always a constant constant represented by the Greek letter pi. We calculate the circumference using the formula: two multiplied by pi multiplied by the radius of the circle. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step. Practice it once with a neat diagram or number line.

lessons.title: Area of a Circular Region
lessons.explanation: The area of a circle represents the total flat surface space enclosed within its boundary. It is calculated using the formula: pi multiplied by the square of the radius. This calculation is highly useful for designing circular gardens, calculating wheel rotations, and manufacturing mechanical washers. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step. Compare two different examples so you can see what changes and what always stays the same.

lessons.title: Conversion of Units and Pathway Areas
lessons.explanation: Calculating pathways involves finding the area of rectangular borders, margins, or circular paths. We must also convert area units, such as converting square centimeters to square meters. One hectare equals ten thousand square meters, a standard metric conversion used for measuring large agricultural farmlands. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step. Compare two different examples so you can see what changes and what always stays the same.

Class 7 - Mathematics - Algebraic Expres.content: Algebraic Expressions allow us to write mathematical rules and formulas in a compact, universal language using variables and constants. You will learn to identify terms, factors, and coefficients, and perform addition and subtraction on algebraic terms. This chapter builds the analytical skills needed to solve advanced math problems.

lessons.title: Terms, Factors, and Coefficients
lessons.explanation: An algebraic expression is built from parts called terms, which are added together. Terms themselves are formed by multiplying factors, which can be variables or numerical constants. The numerical factor in a term is called the coefficient, which is crucial for identifying values. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step. Compare two different examples so you can see what changes and what always stays the same.

lessons.title: Like and Unlike Terms
lessons.explanation: Like terms are mathematical terms that have the exact same algebraic factors, meaning their variable parts are identical. Unlike terms have different algebraic factors. Only like terms can be added or subtracted together, making the simplification of complex algebraic expressions logical and systematic. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step. Compare two different examples so you can see what changes and what always stays the same.

lessons.title: Addition and Subtraction of Expressions
lessons.explanation: Adding and subtracting algebraic expressions involves grouping all the like terms together and performing arithmetic operations on their numerical coefficients. Unlike terms are left unchanged. This process simplifies multi-variable expressions, turning complex mathematical phrases into simple, elegant equations. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step. Try drawing the idea, checking the rule, and explaining the answer in your own words after solving it.

lessons.title: Finding Value of an Expression
lessons.explanation: We evaluate an algebraic expression by substituting specific integers or fractions for the variables. By replacing letters with numbers and following the order of operations, we calculate the final numerical value of the expression, a process used constantly in physics formulas and computer programming. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step. Compare two different examples so you can see what changes and what always stays the same.

Class 7 - Mathematics - Exponents and Po.content: Exponents and Powers provide a shorthand notation for writing and calculating extremely large or tiny numbers, such as the distance between planets or the size of cells. This chapter teaches you base-exponent notation, the fundamental laws of exponents, and how to express numbers in standard scientific notation.

lessons.title: Understanding Exponential Notation
lessons.explanation: Exponential notation is used to represent the repeated multiplication of a number by itself. In the term five raised to the power of three, five is the base and three is the exponent. This notation makes extremely large numbers easy to write, read, and calculate. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step. Compare two different examples so you can see what changes and what always stays the same.

lessons.title: Laws of Exponents: Part 1
lessons.explanation: Laws of exponents simplify calculations. When multiplying powers with the same base, we add their exponents. When dividing powers with the same base, we subtract the divisor's exponent from the dividend's. Raising a power to another power involves multiplying the two exponents together. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step. Compare two different examples so you can see what changes and what always stays the same.

lessons.title: Laws of Exponents: Part 2
lessons.explanation: When multiplying or dividing powers with different bases but the same exponents, we multiply or divide the bases first and keep the common exponent. Furthermore, any non-zero number raised to the power of zero is mathematically equal to one, a fundamental rule of algebra. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step. Compare two different examples so you can see what changes and what always stays the same.

lessons.title: Standard Scientific Notation
lessons.explanation: Scientific notation represents very large or small numbers in a standard format: a decimal between one and ten multiplied by a power of ten. This standard form is used by astronomers, scientists, and engineers to write stellar distances and microscopic measurements easily. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step. Try drawing the idea, checking the rule, and explaining the answer in your own words after solving it.

Class 7 - Mathematics - Symmetry.content: Symmetry is a beautiful, balanced proportion found abundantly in nature, art, and architecture. In this chapter, you will study line symmetry (reflectional symmetry) and rotational symmetry in regular polygons. Recognizing symmetry develops your artistic eye and spatial visualization skills.

lessons.title: Line Symmetry in Regular Polygons
lessons.explanation: A figure has line symmetry if an imaginary line divides it into two halves that are perfect mirror reflections of each other. A regular polygon with n sides always has exactly n lines of symmetry, such as an equilateral triangle having three lines of symmetry. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step. Compare two different examples so you can see what changes and what always stays the same.

lessons.title: Understanding Rotational Symmetry
lessons.explanation: A geometric figure possesses rotational symmetry if it looks exactly the same as its original position more than once during a complete three hundred and sixty-degree rotation around its central point. The number of times it matches is called the order of rotational symmetry. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step. Compare two different examples so you can see what changes and what always stays the same.

lessons.title: Angle and Order of Rotation
lessons.explanation: The fixed point around which a shape rotates is the center of rotation. The minimum angle required to make the shape look identical to its start position is the angle of rotation. For a square, the angle is ninety degrees, and its order of rotation is four. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step. Practice it once with a neat diagram or number line.

lessons.title: Symmetry in Art and Everyday Life
lessons.explanation: Symmetry is a fundamental concept applied in daily life. Architects use line and rotational symmetry to design structurally balanced buildings, while artists use it to create beautiful Rangoli designs, repeating textile patterns, national flags, and decorative corporate logos, creating visual harmony. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step. Try drawing the idea, checking the rule, and explaining the answer in your own words after solving it.

Class 7 - Mathematics - Visualising Soli.content: We live in a three-dimensional world, yet we represent it on two-dimensional screens and papers. This chapter teaches you how to visualize and draw solid shapes. You will study faces, edges, and vertices of polyhedrons, explore nets for building 3D solids, and learn to draw oblique and isometric sketches.

lessons.title: Faces, Edges, and Vertices
lessons.explanation: Three-dimensional solid shapes have unique structural parts. The flat surfaces are called faces, the line segments where two faces meet are called edges, and the corner points where three or more edges meet are called vertices, which help classify polyhedrons like prisms. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step. Try drawing the idea, checking the rule, and explaining the answer in your own words after solving it.

lessons.title: Nets for Building 3D Solids
lessons.explanation: A net is a two-dimensional skeleton outline or flat template that can be folded along its edges to construct a perfect three-dimensional solid shape. Engineers and packaging designers use nets to construct boxes, cardboard containers, cylinders, and pyramids from flat sheets. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step. Try drawing the idea, checking the rule, and explaining the answer in your own words after solving it.

lessons.title: Oblique and Isometric Sketches
lessons.explanation: Oblique sketches are drawn on squared paper, showing solid shapes without keeping exact proportional dimensions. Isometric sketches are drawn on dot sheets, maintaining correct proportional measurements and angles, allowing us to represent three-dimensional structures accurately on flat sheets of paper. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step. Try drawing the idea, checking the rule, and explaining the answer in your own words after solving it.

lessons.title: Slicing and Viewing Solid Shapes
lessons.explanation: We can visualize three-dimensional shapes in different ways. Slicing a solid horizontally or vertically reveals its flat two-dimensional cross-section. We can also study solids by projecting their shadows under lights or viewing them from different angles: front, side, and top views. Work through one small example as you read, because mathematics becomes clearer when each term is linked to a visible step. Try drawing the idea, checking the rule, and explaining the answer in your own words after solving it.

Class 7 - Science - Nutrition in Plants.content: Plants are the primary food producers of our planet, sustaining almost all living organisms. This chapter explores how plants prepare their own food through photosynthesis using sunlight, chlorophyll, carbon dioxide, and water. You will also study alternative modes of plant nutrition, such as parasitic, insectivorous, and saprotrophic behaviors.

lessons.title: Photosynthesis: Food Making in Plants
lessons.explanation: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants prepare their own food. Using chlorophyll, the green pigment in leaves, plants absorb solar energy to convert carbon dioxide from the air and water from the soil into glucose, releasing oxygen as a vital life-supporting byproduct. Think of one observation from home, school, or nature that shows this idea working in real life. Ask what is happening, why it happens, and how we could test it with a simple activity.

lessons.title: Parasitic and Symbiotic Plants
lessons.explanation: Some plants cannot perform photosynthesis. Parasitic plants like Cuscuta (Amarbel) climb host trees and absorb nutrients, harming the host. In symbiotic relationships like lichens, an alga and a fungus live together, sharing shelter, water, and synthesized food to survive in harsh conditions. Think of one observation from home, school, or nature that shows this idea working in real life. Ask what is happening, why it happens, and how we could test it with a simple activity.

lessons.title: Insectivorous and Saprotrophic Nutrition
lessons.explanation: Insectivorous plants like pitcher plants grow in nitrogen-poor soils and trap insects to meet their nutrient requirements. Saprotrophs, including fungi and mushrooms, grow on decaying matter, releasing digestive juices to dissolve dead organic tissue and absorb nutrients through saprotrophic nutrition. Ask what is happening, why it happens, and how we could test it with a simple activity. Think of one observation from home, school, or nature that shows this idea working in real life. Record one example in your notebook after reading.

lessons.title: Replenishing Nutrients in Soil
lessons.explanation: Farming depletes soil nutrients like nitrogen, potassium, and phosphorus. These are replenished through organic manures, fertilizers, and a natural partnership with Rhizobium bacteria. Living in legume roots, Rhizobium converts atmospheric nitrogen into soluble forms, keeping the soil fertile and healthy naturally. Think of one observation from home, school, or nature that shows this idea working in real life. Ask what is happening, why it happens, and how we could test it with a simple activity. Record one example in your notebook after reading.

Class 7 - Science - Nutrition in Animals.content: Unlike plants, animals cannot make their own food and must consume other organisms to gain energy and nutrients. This chapter covers the fascinating processes of animal nutrition, focusing on human digestion, the digestive systems of grass-eating animals (ruminants), and how single-celled organisms like Amoeba feed and survive.

lessons.title: Steps in Animal Nutrition
lessons.explanation: Animal nutrition is a multi-step process. It begins with ingestion (taking in food), followed by mechanical and chemical digestion (breaking food into simple substances), absorption into blood vessels, assimilation (using nutrients for growth), and egestion of undigested waste. Think of one observation from home, school, or nature that shows this idea working in real life. Ask what is happening, why it happens, and how we could test it with a simple activity. Record one example in your notebook after reading.

lessons.title: The Human Digestive System
lessons.explanation: The human digestive tract consists of the buccal cavity, food pipe, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, and rectum. The stomach secretes acids, while the liver and pancreas produce digestive juices that break down proteins, carbohydrates, and fats in the small intestine. Ask what is happening, why it happens, and how we could test it with a simple activity. Think of one observation from home, school, or nature that shows this idea working in real life. Record one example in your notebook after reading.

lessons.title: Digestion in Grass-Eating Ruminants
lessons.explanation: Grass-eating animals like cows are called ruminants. They swallow grass quickly without chewing, storing it in a stomach chamber called the rumen. Here, bacteria digest cellulose, forming cud, which the animal regurgitates in small lumps to chew thoroughly later. Think of one observation from home, school, or nature that shows this idea working in real life. Ask what is happening, why it happens, and how we could test it with a simple activity. Record one example in your notebook after reading.

lessons.title: Feeding and Digestion in Amoeba
lessons.explanation: Amoeba is a microscopic, single-celled organism found in pond water. When it senses food, it pushes out finger-like projections called pseudopodia (false feet) to surround the food particle, trapping it in a food vacuole where digestive juices digest it. Think of one observation from home, school, or nature that shows this idea working in real life. Ask what is happening, why it happens, and how we could test it with a simple activity. Record one example in your notebook after reading.
